data.name: Rictor
data.description: Defining subunit of mTORC2 (Rapamycin-Insensitive Companion of mTOR); routes mTOR toward Akt and the cytoskeleton rather than S6K1/4E-BP1.
data.description_beginner: The defining building block of mTORC2 (the second mTOR complex) - without it, you don't have mTORC2. It steers mTOR signaling toward Akt and the cell's internal skeleton rather than toward growth/protein-building.

reading_levels.beginner: The part that makes mTOR into mTORC2.
reading_levels.research: Confers acute rapamycin insensitivity and, with SIN1, the substrate specificity for Akt S473.

studies.title: Rictor, a novel binding partner of mTOR, defines a rapamycin-insensitive and raptor-independent pathway that regulates the cytoskeleton
studies.authors: Sarbassov DD; Ali SM; Kim DH; Guertin DA; Latek RR; Erdjument-Bromage H; Tempst P; Sabatini DM

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Discovery of Rictor and the SECOND mTOR complex, mTORC2. Crucially showed this complex is NOT blocked by rapamycin and does not use Raptor - it controls the cytoskeleton via PKC. This is the paper that split mTOR biology into 'two faces' at the molecular level.

studies.title: Prolonged rapamycin treatment inhibits mTORC2 assembly and Akt/PKB
studies.authors: Sarbassov DD; Ali SM; Sengupta S; Sheen JH; Hsu PP; Bagley AF; Markhard AL; Sabatini DM

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: The molecular explanation for rapamycin's dark side. Short-term rapamycin only hits mTORC1, but prolonged treatment can also inhibit the assembly of NEW mTORC2 in susceptible cell types, reducing mTORC2 abundance and cutting Akt signaling over time. The wording matters: this is prevention of new assembly, not the dismantling of complexes already built, and the response depends on cell context and length of exposure. This is the mechanistic root of the insulin-resistance side effect later shown in mice (see Lamming 2012) - crucial for anyone dosing rapamycin for longevity.

studies.title: Ablation in mice of the mTORC components raptor, rictor, or mLST8 reveals that mTORC2 is required for signaling to Akt-FOXO and PKCalpha, but not S6K1
studies.authors: Guertin DA; Stevens DM; Thoreen CC; Burds AA; Kalaany NY; Moffat J; Brown M; Fitzgerald KJ; Sabatini DM

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: The foundational genetic 'dissection' of the two complexes in living mice. Deleting Raptor was lethal early (mTORC1 essential); deleting Rictor or mLST8 selectively knocked out mTORC2 signaling to Akt and PKCalpha but spared S6K1. This cleanly assigned jobs to each complex and showed mLST8 is an mTORC2-specific requirement in mice.

studies.title: mTORC2 controls actin polymerization required for consolidation of long-term memory
studies.authors: Huang W; Zhu PJ; Zhang S; Zhou H; Stoica L; Galiano M; Krnjevic K; Roman G; Costa-Mattioli M

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Conditional Rictor-knockout mice (postnatal forebrain) and Drosophila
studies.finding: Conditional deletion of Rictor in the postnatal mouse forebrain reduced mTORC2 activity and selectively impaired long-term memory and the late phase of hippocampal LTP, with a comparable long-term-memory deficit in dTORC2-deficient flies. Hippocampal actin polymerisation was reduced, and restoring it rescued both L-LTP and long-term memory; a compound that raised mTORC2 activity converted early LTP into late LTP and enhanced memory. This is the loss-of-function AND rescue evidence that mTORC2 is required for memory consolidation - the arm chronic rapamycin also disrupts, and the study Open Question H8 needs for its mTORC2 liability leg, which until 2026-09-05 rested on no supporting study at all.

studies.title: Skeletal muscle-specific ablation of raptor, but not of rictor, causes metabolic changes and results in muscle dystrophy
studies.authors: Bentzinger CF; Romanino K; Cloëtta D; Lin S; Mascarenhas JB; Oliveri F; Xia J; Casanova E; Costa CF; Brink M; Zorzato F; Hall MN; Rueegg MA

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: In mice, muscle-specific raptor loss (not rictor) causes dystrophy, showing mTORC1 is essential for muscle homeostasis.

studies.title: PTEN regulates microtubule polymerization via mTORC2, but not mTORC1, in peripheral sensory neurons
studies.authors: Evans S; Reglewski J; Rose H; Lewis C; Nayak A; Minsky C; McNeil E; Knowles B; Wang W; Li M; Luikart BW; Hong J

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Mouse peripheral sensory neuron cultures (Pten-KO with Raptor or Rictor co-deletion, both sexes)
studies.finding: Uses Raptor (mTORC1) versus Rictor (mTORC2) co-deletion on a Pten-knockout background to ask which complex carries the growth signal to the microtubule cytoskeleton. Suppressing mTORC2 — but not mTORC1 — returns the accelerated microtubule polymerisation and neuronal hypertrophy of Pten-KO neurons to wild-type levels, and the effect is confined to the axonal growth cone rather than the proximal axon shaft. A clean genetic dissection on the comparatively thin mTORC2 side of the pathway.

studies.title: Pdcd4-Rictor interaction suppresses mTORC2-PFKFB3 axis and tumorigenesis in NSCLC.
studies.authors: Wang Q; Xin Y; Zokaei E; Zeng L; Piecoro D; Chen M; Zhang Y; Yang KS; Wang C; Liu X; Yang HS

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: NSCLC cell lines; mouse xenograft; human tumour tissue
studies.finding: Pdcd4 binds Rictor via residues R105/K108/R110 to disrupt mTORC2 assembly and kinase activity, lowering PFKFB3 levels and suppressing glycolysis and NSCLC tumour growth.

studies.title: The role of mTORC2/RICTOR in immune cells and inflammatory diseases.
studies.authors: Xu J; Zhong W; Xin F; Xu F; Zheng Z; Guo F

evidence.label: Review — secondary literature, not a new result
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Review of immune cell subsets (T cells, B cells, macrophages, dendritic cells, NK cells) and mouse conditional-knockout models
studies.finding: mTORC2/RICTOR signaling (via AKT, SGK1, PKC) shapes Th1/Th2 differentiation, Treg stability, memory T cell formation, BCR signaling and plasma cell survival, and macrophage/DC/NK function; its role in tissue inflammation is context-dependent (exacerbating osteoarthritis and pancreatitis but restraining pro-inflammatory polarization in colorectal cancer), and dual mTORC1/2 inhibitors (e.g. AZD2014) show early but complicated promise.

studies.title: The mammalian target of rapamycin complex 2 controls folding and stability of Akt and protein kinase C
studies.authors: Facchinetti V; Ouyang W; Wei H; Soto N; Lazorchak A; Gould C; Lowry C; Newton AC; Mao Y; Miao RQ; Sessa WC; Qin J; Zhang P; Su B; Jacinto E

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Mouse embryonic fibroblasts lacking mTORC2 components (SIN1, rictor, mTOR) and human cell lines; yeast; mouse tissue; in vitro kinase assays
studies.finding: Cells lacking the mTORC2 components mTOR, SIN1 or rictor lost phosphorylation of Akt and of conventional protein kinase C at the turn motif, a site near the end of the kinase domain. This phosphorylation did not depend on growth factors, and the authors reported the same function in yeast. Turn-motif phosphorylation helped newly made Akt and PKC fold correctly and stay stable; without it, Akt was held by the chaperone Hsp90 and protected from ubiquitin-mediated breakdown. mTORC2 controlled the Akt turn-motif and hydrophobic-motif (Ser473) sites independently in vivo and phosphorylated both directly in vitro. Boundary: Cell culture, yeast and in vitro kinase assays, with mouse tissue for the in vivo site analysis. Shows a protein-maturation role of mTORC2, not an organismal phenotype. Drafted from the abstract only.

studies.title: Hepatic mTORC2 activates glycolysis and lipogenesis through Akt, glucokinase, and SREBP1c
studies.authors: Hagiwara A; Cornu M; Cybulski N; Polak P; Betz C; Trapani F; Terracciano L; Heim MH; Rüegg MA; Hall MN

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Liver-specific rictor knockout mice (LiRiKO); primary hepatocytes with constitutively active Akt2 or glucokinase rescue
studies.finding: The authors deleted rictor, an essential mTORC2 component, only in mouse liver. In fed knockout mice the liver lost Akt Ser473 phosphorylation and had lower glucokinase and SREBP1c activity, so it kept making glucose (gluconeogenesis) while glycolysis and fat synthesis fell, as if it could not sense that the animal had eaten. The mice became hyperglycaemic and hyperinsulinaemic with low blood lipids. In mTORC2-deficient hepatocytes, constitutively active Akt2 restored both glucose flux and lipogenesis, while extra glucokinase restored glucose flux but not lipogenesis, placing Akt as the main route from hepatic mTORC2 to these outputs. Boundary: Mouse liver with lifelong genetic loss of mTORC2, plus cultured mouse hepatocytes. Not a drug study and not tested in people. Drafted from the abstract only.

studies.title: mTORC1 and mTORC2 selectively regulate CD8+ T cell differentiation
studies.authors: Pollizzi KN; Patel CH; Sun IH; Oh MH; Waickman AT; Wen J; Delgoffe GM; Powell JD

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Mice with T-cell-specific deletion of Tsc2, Rheb or Rictor (and Tsc2/Rictor double knockout), OT-I adoptive transfer, vaccinia-OVA and Listeria-OVA infection, EL4 and B16-OVA tumour models, rapamycin (100 ug/kg/day) and 2-deoxyglucose in vivo, Seahorse metabolic profiling
studies.finding: By deleting Tsc2, Rheb or Rictor in T cells, this work split the CD8 response between the two mTOR complexes. Tsc2 loss left mTORC1 constitutively active: the cells were strongly glycolytic (high ECAR, high Slc2a1 and Pfk1, low spare respiratory capacity), made more IFN-gamma, TNF and granzyme B, cleared EL4 thymoma and slowed B16-OVA growth, but stayed terminally differentiated and were about two-fold fewer than wild type at day 30, with no memory. Rheb loss removed mTORC1 activity with mTORC2 intact: those cells failed as effectors but kept memory-like features and were about two-fold more numerous at day 30, yet did not respond to rechallenge, which the authors trace to metabolic defects. Rapamycin from day 5 (100 ug/kg daily) rescued survival of Tsc2-deficient cells, raised CD127 and Eomesodermin, lowered KLRG1 and T-bet and restored a recall response. Losing mTORC2 by Rictor deletion left effector function intact but increased memory cells that still responded 133 days after infection, and the Tsc2/Rictor double knockout showed that the hyperactive effector phenotype needs mTORC2. Boundary: mouse genetics with TCR-transgenic transfers and transplantable tumours; the comparison rests on genetic extremes (no TSC2, no Rheb, no Rictor) rather than graded physiological signalling, and nothing here is measured in people.

relations.mechanism: Rictor defines the second complex, mTORC2, which rapamycin does not block acutely.
relations.mechanism_beginner: Rictor is what makes the second complex, mTORC2, distinct – and rapamycin doesn't block it right away.
relations.boundary: Mammalian cells, Drosophila and conditional Rictor-knockout mice (SAR2004, JAC2004, HUA2013). Shows that the complex needs Rictor; relevance in human tissue is not tested by these studies.
